name: Clickfacts
long_description: ClickFacts is a Malware Software Solutions company for buyers and sellers of online media. Its automated plug and play malware discovery solution tests online ads (SWFs & 3rd Party Ad Tags) and web pages within websites to ensure they do not distribute malware onto usersâ€™ computers (which can lead to identity theft). Its moderation software solution monitors websites to ensure the ads running on them are free of inappropriate content (e.g., nudity, racism), and its Ad Buddy product provides to advertisers real-time continuous monitoring and a complete history of where their ads have run. ClickFacts Inc. was founded in 2005 by Mikhail Ledvich, Mikhail Gurevich, and Greg Gurevich in Boston Mass, with initial funding by YCombinator. It is now based in San Francisco, California.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada

business_model: B2B software subscription for ad verification and monitoring (pricing not verified)
product_category: Ad verification, click fraud and malvertising detection
founder_names: Mikhail Ledvich; Mikhail Gurevich; Greg Gurevich
market_need_then: Click fraud was a widely covered concern in 2006, with one report of Google crediting an advertiser for clicks that Clickfacts flagged, and vendors reporting double digit fraud rates.
outcome_analysis: Clickfacts began in the 2005 YC batch selling click fraud detection into a loudly discussed 2006 market and later broadened to ad network verification, malware discovery and moderation. YC lists it as acquired, but no acquirer, date or price turned up, so the exit quality and cause cannot be judged from public sources.

name: Kiko
one_liner: We're the best online calendar solution to ever exist. Period.
long_description:
Kiko is a web calendar for anyone who wants to keep and share a calendar online. Kiko excels at three main things:

* Universal access: Kiko integrates with your mobile phone and AIM and lets you access your calendar from any computer.

* Share your calendar: Invite anyone to events (not just other Kiko users!) Let others view your calendar with just a click.

* As easy as paper - or maybe easier: Write "Pay gas bill every month" onto your calendar and watch Kiko do the Right Thing!
all_locations: Boston, MA, USA; Cambridge, MA, USA
regions: United States of America; America / Canada

business_model: Free consumer web app, no revenue model documented

outcome_analysis: Kiko launched an Ajax calendar in August 2005 to good early reviews but competed against Google Calendar, which arrived in 2006 and matched its features. The founders listed the company on eBay and Tucows won it on 2006-08-26 to bring calendar features to its email platform, a feature purchase rather than a venture outcome. The founders moved on to Justin.tv.

name: Loopt
long_description:
Loopt, based in Silicon-Valley and backed by leading venture capital firms Sequoia Capital and New Enterprise Associates, has created an interoperable social-mapping service that allows individuals to use their location to discover the real world around them – enabling them to find and enjoy the people, places, and events that mean the most right here and now using their mobile phones. 

With Loopt, individuals will always know who’s around, what to do, or where to go
all_locations: San Francisco, CA, USA; Mountain View, CA, USA
regions: United States of America; America / Canada

business_model: Carrier distributed subscription and later free app with location advertising
product_category: Mobile social mapping
founder_names: Sam Altman; Nick Sivo; Alok Deshpande
market_need_then: Carriers launched social mapping in 2006 (Boost Mobile with Loopt, Helio Buddy Beacon), and press covered the appeal and privacy debate; users reached 4 million by July 2010.
outcome_analysis: Loopt raised venture rounds from Sequoia and NEA, distributed through carriers such as Boost and Sprint, and reached 4 million users by 2010. Location sharing then moved into larger platforms and phones, and Loopt sold to Green Dot in March 2012 for 43.4 million dollars cash, of which 9.8 million was a retention pool, which looks like a team and technology acquisition more than a growth outcome.

name: Reddit

one_liner: The frontpage of the internet.
long_description:
Founded by Steve Huffman and Alexis Ohanian in 2005, Reddit is an online community where users submit, vote, and comment on content, news, and discussions. Nicknamed "the front page of the internet,"​ Reddit is one of the top ten sites in the United States (source: Alexa), with hundreds of millions of users each month on desktop, mobile web, and our official Android/iOS apps. 

Interested in joining our growing team? Check out about.reddit.com/careers
regions: United States of America; America / Canada

business_model: Advertising, later data licensing and premium subscriptions
product_category: Social news and community platform
market_need_then: Del.icio.us/popular and Digg showed demand for community ranked links in 2005; Reddit's founders pitched against Slashdot and del.icio.us after YC redirected their food ordering idea.
outcome_analysis: Reddit launched in June 2005 about three weeks into the first YC batch and was sold to Condé Nast in October 2006 for a reported $10M to $20M with under $50,000 monthly revenue. Advance spun it out, it raised $50M in 2014 and $200M at $1.8B in 2017, and it listed in March 2024 raising $600M. Community network effects and a distinctive brand drove the outcome while rival Digg faded.

name: TextPayMe
long_description:
Founded in 2005, TextPayMe is an SMS payment service that lets you send money to other people using cell phone text messaging. TextPayMe lets you send money to anyone else in the US with an SMS-capable cell phone, and while phone carriers may charge for the actual text message sent/received, sending and receiving money is free while TextPayMe remains in Beta.

In July 2006, the TextPayMe team started working for Amazon and, as of 2011, the site redirects to an Amazon's mobile payment website. There was no press release related to this event but it's assumed the company was acquired.

Sending and receiving payments through TextPayMe is easy: simply write a text message to SMS@TextPayMe.com with "pay amount phonenumber" in the body (i.e. to send $5 to 123-456-7890, text "pay 5 1234567890"). The service is secure as well, as each payment needs to be confirmed by a user-created PIN. To fund your transactions, TextPayMe lets you add money directly from your bank account and now also lets you link your credit card as well. Currently, the maximum amount that can be sent or received per month is $500.
all_locations: Seattle, WA, USA; Redmond, WA, USA
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: US consumers splitting bills or sending small sums by SMS
problem: Sending small amounts of money to friends, such as splitting a restaurant bill, was awkward.
business_model: Free during beta, planned fees on SMS payments, monthly cap of 500 dollars
product_category: SMS peer to peer payments
founder_names: Philip Yuen; Gerald Yuen; CJ Huang
market_need_then: Press in 2006 pitched it as eliminating the IOU between friends, and PayPal and Obopay both entered the same year, though Failory notes US peer to peer payments had not yet taken off.
outcome_analysis: TextPayMe launched its SMS payment beta in December 2005, got early press, and within months faced PayPal Mobile and Obopay. The team started working at Amazon in July 2006 and the site later redirected to Amazon Payments, which looks like a soft landing rather than a venture exit. No press release or price was found.

name: Clustrix
long_description:
Clustrix provides the leading scale-out relational database engineered for the cloud or data center. ClustrixDB is a drop-in replacement for MySQL and an ideal solution for high-transaction, high-value workloads typically found in businesses such as ad tech, e-commerce, gaming, and large web and mobile businesses.

Our customers use ClustrixDB for critical business applications that support massive transactional volume. ClustrixDB delivers more than twenty-five trillion transactions per month for customers including AOL, Nielsen, Match, MakeMyTrip, Photobox, Rakuten, and Symantec.

Headquartered in San Francisco, Clustrix is funded by HighBar Partners, Sequoia Capital, U.S. Venture Partners, ATA Ventures, and Y Combinator. ClustrixDB is available in software that runs on commodity hardware and on any cloud.

Visit www.clustrix.com to learn more.

Follow @Clustrix on Twitter and "like"​ us on Facebook!

#BetterSQL
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: High-transaction web, ad tech, e-commerce and gaming companies running MySQL
problem: MySQL workloads outgrew single servers and sharding was painful; customers needed a scale-out relational database.
business_model: Enterprise database software and appliances, licensing and support
product_category: Scale-out relational database (NewSQL)
market_need_then: MySQL scale limits were a common web company pain in the late 2000s; customers named later included AOL, Nielsen and Match.
outcome_analysis: Clustrix spent years building a scale-out MySQL-compatible database, launched it around 2010 and raised venture money through 2013, reaching about 51 staff. It was acquired by MariaDB on 2018-09-20 at an undisclosed price and later folded into Xpand, which MariaDB announced as discontinued in October 2023. A hard technical product found customers but never broke out against cloud databases.

name: Project Wedding
long_description:
Finding wedding vendors is hard. In 2007, a couple started Project Wedding to tackle this problem and eventually grew it into a full-featured wedding planning site. Now part of the WeddingWire Network, Project Wedding strives to make wedding planning easier, less stressful, and more fun!

Over 1 million brides come to Project Wedding monthly to interact with our supportive community and to read our curated editorial content. We know that today's weddings are all about showing off personal style with creative elements, gorgeous color palettes, and unique details. We also know that the contemporary bride is incredibly busy and wants to take care of all of her wedding planning needs in one spot. Enter Project Wedding!

product_category: Online wedding planning

regions: United States of America; America / Canada; Remote; Partly Remote

It later turned the corpus into a subscription library, took Khosla money in 2015 and $58M in 2019, bought SlideShare in 2020, and remains active with 300 staff. Success came from owning search traffic for documents, then pivoting to paid content.

name: Wufoo
one_liner: Online form builder.
long_description:
Wufoo is a web application that helps anybody build amazing online forms. When you design a form with Wufoo, it automatically builds the database, backend and scripts needed to make collecting and understanding your data easy, fast and fun. No coding required! 

Founded in 2006, Wufoo was created by Chris Campbell, Kevin Hale and Ryan Campbell on the belief that forms were the starting point for building anything useful on the web. The problem they saw was that one of the most efficient and used interfaces for collecting data, wasn’t very efficient to create. So they decide to fix that by creating Wufoo!

In 2011, Wufoo was acquired by SurveyMonkey, the leader in web-based survey solutions, to help complement their growing suite of services to offer amazing data collections tools to their customers.

product_category: Online form builder
founder_names: Chris Campbell; Kevin Hale; Ryan Campbell

outcome_analysis: Wufoo launched in July 2006 after raising only about $118,000 and never raised again. The product reached enough paying users that SurveyMonkey bought it on 2011-04-25 for a reported $35M in cash and stock. A cheap, focused SaaS with strong design reached an acquisition without venture rounds, and it still runs under SurveyMonkey.

name: Appjet
long_description:
Y Combinator funded AppJet is an online programming tool for building simple web apps. Founded by former MIT students, AppJet intends to simplify the process of writing web applications. The applications are programmed on a web based text editor in the simple but powerful JavaScript programming language. JavaScript is used on both the server and client side. They've included several bundles of code libraries for databases and more importantly interfacing with the Facebook API. In order to efficiently host users' applications, AppJet has developed their own application virtualization system. The system allocates processor time to active applications and cuts off greedy ones after running an alloted number of compiled lines of code to prevent abuse.

AppJet as a dev platform seems no longer to be active. There are some legacy downloads available, however.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: Programmers and hobbyists building simple web apps in JavaScript
problem: Writing and hosting a web application required setting up servers and stacks. AppJet offered an in-browser editor and hosting using JavaScript on both client and server.
business_model: free hosted development platform, no revenue model found
product_category: online web app development platform (later collaborative editor EtherPad)
market_need_then: Developer interest in simple hosted web app tools was present in 2007, but the team found more traction with the EtherPad demo app, which was seen as a threat to Google Docs.
outcome_analysis: AppJet entered YC in Summer 2007 with a hosted JavaScript platform, launched a public beta in December 2007, then pivoted toward its EtherPad real-time editor demo. After closing a roughly 250 thousand dollar angel round led by Mitch Kapor in 2009, Google acquired it on December 4, 2009 to join the Wave team and later open sourced the code.

name: Auctomatic
long_description:
Auctomatic, a Y Combinator company, offers an auction and marketplace management system for all of those individual sellers on such sites as Ebay, Amazon, Overstock and others. The application lets you list your items as well as manage your sales, but it also helps you understand how to best optimize your selling and maximize profits.

The company also received an investment from Paul Buchheit, the lead developer of Gmail.

product_category: Multi-marketplace seller inventory and listing tools
founder_names: Kulveer Taggar; Harjeet Taggar; Patrick Collison
market_need_then: eBay and multi-marketplace selling was large by 2007, and a cottage industry of third-party listing and management services (Vendio, Marketworks, ChannelAdvisor) existed, showing sellers paid for tooling; no direct usage figures for Auctomatic were found.
outcome_analysis: Auctomatic was a two-to-three person Winter 2007 team, partly the Collison brothers' Shuppa merged with the Taggar brothers, that shipped a multi-marketplace seller inventory beta in October 2007 and sold to Communicate.com (Live Current Media) for about $5M in cash and stock in March 2008, roughly a year after founding. The wedge was copyable and sat among established seller-tool vendors, so a quick strategic sale to a domain-and-web company that wanted to move into products looks like a modest, soft-landing-style exit; the price is press-reported and the product did not continue as an independent business.

name: ContestMachine
one_liner: Roll your own contest or giveaway.  No longer in business.
long_description: ContestMachine is a web service that makes running promotions from any website easy. The service allows clients to run a contest or giveaway from their blog or website and handles the rest of the details, like collecting submissions and contacting winners. The service also allows clients varied options, like choosing entry requirements, start and end times, and the addition of prizes.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada

name: Disqus
one_liner: Add comments to your website.
long_description: We love the internet, and the colorful characters and interesting conversations that make up its diverse communities. Disqus exists to make better communities and an even better web. Today, our product ecosystem includes our established comment network (over 4 million websites that cover pretty much any topic imaginable), a growing advertising network, and our owned and operated platform. Originally founded in 2007 by CEO Daniel Ha and CTO Jason Yan, we’re changing the way people get into discussions about the things they love -- or are just curious about.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: Bloggers and publishers who wanted a hosted comment system, later advertisers via an ad network
problem: Blog comments were siloed and hard to manage. Disqus gave sites a drop-in threaded comment system with a portable identity.
business_model: free embedded comments monetized by advertising and premium plans
product_category: third-party commenting platform
market_need_then: Third-party comment systems were a crowded and discussed category in 2007 as bloggers wanted richer comment features and identity.
outcome_analysis: Disqus launched in October 2007 into a crowded field of comment systems, raised a half million in 2008 and a 10 million round in 2011, and spread through an embedded logo on over 4 million sites. Zeta Global bought it in December 2017 for a reported 90 million dollars, after a 2017 breach, and a later Norwegian privacy penalty proposal followed.

name: Dropbox
one_liner: Backup and share files in the cloud.
long_description:
Dropbox is building the world’s first smart workspace.
Back in 2007, making work better for people meant designing a simpler way to keep files in sync. Today, it means designing products that reduce busywork so you can focus on the work that matters.

Most “productivity tools” get in your way. They constantly ping, distract, and disrupt your team’s flow, so you spend your days switching between apps and tracking down feedback. It’s busywork, not the meaningful stuff. We want to change this. 

We believe there’s a more enlightened way to work. Dropbox helps people be organized, stay focused, and get in sync with their teams.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: Individuals and prosumers first, then teams and businesses paying for storage and collaboration
problem: People carried files on USB sticks or emailed themselves; existing backup and sync tools were heavyweight and did not just work across machines.
business_model: freemium subscription with referral-driven growth, paid storage tiers and team plans
product_category: file sync and cloud storage
market_need_then: YC application argued existing tools were heavyweight; Dropbox's 2007 demo drew strong interest from developers and the press.
success_factors: strong_pmf; product_led_growth; technical_moat; switching_costs; timing_tailwind; brand_pull; founder_market_fit
outcome_analysis: Dropbox solved file sync better than 2007 incumbents and grew through word of mouth, raising a $250M round at a reported $4B in 2011 and going public in March 2018. Free substitutes from big platforms and macro headwinds slowed growth; it cut about 16% of staff in 2023 and about 20% in October 2024. Rivals recorded here rather than as competition at founding: Mozy and Carbonite (online backup), Box.net, and Microsoft SkyDrive, Groove and FolderShare, whose only sources found are retrospective pages dated years after the 2007 batch.

name: Hello Chair
long_description:
Hello, Chair Inc. was founded in 2006 by Luke Iannini, Mike Jacobs and Kevin Corcoran to explore opportunities in applied machine learning and internet advertising. After receiving funding from Y-Combinator in 2007, we produced Adpinion, one of the first advertising networks to utilize user feedback to drive personalized targeting.

Our core technology — the recommendation engine called SparseReduce — has since proved infinitely adaptable in such diverse problem domains as Amazon product recommendation, eBay auction discovery, image and language comprehension, and Twitter stream exploration.

The latest application of SparseReduce is Appsaurus, an app discovery platform which was released on the eve of 2010 to overwhelming critical acclaim.

We're backed by some pretty incredible investors: Harrison Metal, Mitch Kapor, Chris Sacca, Y-Combinator and David Parker to name a few. We're also proud to have Alexis Ohanian as an advisor.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada

name: Heysan
one_liner: Free messaging on mobile phones
long_description:
Heysan was a free mobile messaging and community based in San Francisco, California.

Initially Heysan provided free messaging between phones and computers, bridging IM with SMS. The service expanded into launching a mobile community and has over 1 million users doing tens of million of monthly messages. In the summer of 2007 Heysan raised a seed round from Khosla Ventures and Atomico, the venture funds of Vinod Khosla and Niklas Zennstrom.

Heysan was acquired by Good Technology in May 2009.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: Mobile phone users who wanted free messaging between phones and computers
problem: SMS cost money and mobile IM was clunky. Heysan bridged IM and SMS with free messaging and a mobile community.
business_model: free consumer mobile messaging with no clear revenue model
product_category: mobile messaging and community
founder_names: Gustaf Alstromer; Marie Brattberg; Pär Lindhe; Parham Michael Ossareh
market_need_then: A 2007 review cited M:Metrics data that 6.3 percent of US mobile subscribers used mobile IM versus 41.1 percent who sent SMS, showing paid SMS dominated.
outcome_analysis: Heysan joined YC in Winter 2007, raised a seed round from Khosla Ventures and Atomico that summer, and grew past one million users, then was acquired by Good Technology in May 2009. Terms are not public, the product disappeared, and smartphone messaging apps soon made SMS bridges less relevant, so the outcome looks like a modest acquisition.

name: Octopart
one_liner: Octopart is a search engine for electronic components
long_description:
Engineering tools should be as streamlined and smart as everything else in your life: as your phone, as your email, as all the apps that help you manage your day-to-day. Your work should be as efficient as possible so you can generate innovative ideas, design elegant technology, and manufacture at scale, all because you can focus on the right things. There should not be any distractions caused by poorly designed websites, unreliable data, or unwieldy spreadsheets of haphazard electronic component information. You should be able to compare components, find important technical information, and easily grasp the spectrum of parts that will be a match for your design.

This is what Octopart strives for.

Finding electronic component information should not be holding engineers back from bringing ideas to life quickly and efficiently. We believe that pricing, availability, technical specifications, and reference designs should be transparent, fast to find, and easy to understand. That’s why we create powerful, intelligent tools that streamline the engineering workflow and enable fast decision making. Octopart provides accurate and complete data for millions of electronic components in a way that makes it easy to find and compare parts. Focus on the important stuff: building the technology of the future.
all_locations: New York City, NY, USA; New York, NY, USA
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: Electronics engineers and buyers comparing component pricing, availability and specifications
problem: Finding electronic component data across distributors was slow and spread over spreadsheets and poor sites. Octopart indexed pricing, stock and specs for millions of parts.
business_model: search engine monetized by distributor leads and advertising, later data products
product_category: electronic component search engine
founder_names: Sam Wurzel; Harish Agarwal; Andres Morey
market_need_then: The company's own description says engineers lost time to poorly designed supplier sites and haphazard spreadsheets of component data.
outcome_analysis: Octopart entered YC in Winter 2007, raised only about 360 thousand dollars of angel seed by May 2008 according to an aggregator, and grew slowly as a niche search engine for engineers. Altium announced the acquisition on August 14, 2015 and it became a subsidiary, with no price disclosed, which suggests a modest but real exit for a capital efficient company.

name: Parakey
long_description:
Parakey was founded in early 2006 by Blake Ross and Joe Hewitt of Mozilla/Firefox fame. Little has been revealed about what Parakey will actually do, but it has been touted as both a platform and set of applications that will merge the desktop environment with the Web. It has also been described as a Web-based operating system. Great emphasis has been placed on Parakey's potential to make tasks on the computer more intuitive for the average Joe.

Parakey was acquired by Facebook on July 19, 2007.

Sequoia Capital seeded Parakey's operations in early 2005.
all_locations: San Francisco, CA, USA; Mountain View, CA, USA
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: Mainstream computer users, with developers as the platform audience
problem: Desktop files and web information lived in separate worlds; the founders wanted a web-style layer that merged the two and made common tasks more intuitive.
business_model: Unlaunched platform and applications; no revenue model disclosed
product_category: Web operating system / desktop and web platform
market_need_then: Web OS projects were a hot topic in 2006 and the Firefox founders drew press (IEEE Spectrum cover, blog coverage), but no source shows measured customer demand.
outcome_analysis: Parakey was a pre-launch team bet. Blake Ross and Joe Hewitt, known for Firefox, built a web OS concept with Sequoia seed money, and Facebook acquired the company on 2007-07-19 as its first acquisition, with the founders moving to Facebook Platform and site work. The exit reflects founder pedigree and acquihire logic more than product traction.

name: Reble
one_liner: P2P Music Sharing
long_description: Reble offers a software download, only for windows, that allows users to stream music from your friends who also have installed Reble. It launched into public beta on Feb. 5th, 2008, and is a Y Combinator-funded company.
all_locations: Boston, MA, USA; San Francisco, CA, USA
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: Windows music fans who wanted to listen to friends' music libraries
problem: Listeners wanted to play music stored on friends' computers as easily as local files.
business_model: Free desktop client; revenue model not stated
product_category: Peer-to-peer music streaming client
market_need_then: Interest in social music discovery in 2007 and 2008 was high, shown by several competing launches. Legal limits restricted sharing, and Reble streamed only DRM-free MP3s.
outcome_analysis: Reble entered public beta on 5 February 2008 as a Windows only client for streaming friends' music, and is listed by YC as inactive. No shutdown date or cause is public, so the cause is not public and no failure factor is assigned. Comparable services such as Social.FM also closed in 2008, hinting at a hard category, but this is not evidence about Reble itself.

name: Socialmoth
long_description: Socialmoth is a community to post your thoughts anonymously. You can view postings (mostly gossip and secrets) from the whole community as well as get updates for when someone in your group of friends makes a post. The vast majority of their members appear to be women, with over 600 posts being made per day. These guys will also be taking a new spin on their idea, launching Disenchat.com, a place to post anonymously about your workplace. The system will verify your organization by email address (like Facebook) and let you start riffing. Outsiders will be able to see the existence of the forum and volume of posting, but not the specific comments.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada

name: Songkick
long_description:
Songkick is the great live music startup. Since 2007, we’ve set about making it as easy, fun and fair as possible for you to see your favorite artists live. Right now, more than 15 million music fans across the globe use Songkick to track their favorite artists, discover awesome concerts and never ever miss out.

With over 6 million event listings, we’re the biggest concert service on the planet. Across web, iPhone, Android, and through rich partnerships with Spotify, Pandora, Facebook and more, Songkick is the definitive and trusted home for live music online.

We’ve always put fans first. We’re a small, fast-moving team packed to the brim with digital expertise, committed to solving real problems for our users. Live music is for everyone, and we work hard to empower our community, add meaningful value and cut out the BS along the way.

We do our best work when we’re happy, respectful and relaxed. Our values and work ethic have got us far, and as we grow we’ll never shake that small startup feel. Earlier this year we became part of the Warner Music Group family, opening up epic new realms of opportunities to bring fans and artists closer together.

We're hiring: head over to https://www.songkick.com/jobs to see our open roles
regions: United Kingdom; Europe
target_customer: Live music fans (free), monetized via ticketing referral fees, later ticketing and artist tools
problem: Fans missed concerts by their favorite artists because event information was scattered across ticket sites and blogs.
business_model: Ticketing referral fees, later direct ticketing and promoter campaigns
product_category: Concert discovery and ticketing
founder_names: Ian Hogarth; Pete Finlay (born Smith); Michelle You
market_need_then: Fans relied on scattered listings; TechCrunch's launch review in 2007 framed Songkick as a better way to track artists across 14 ticket sites and blogs.
outcome_analysis: Songkick built the largest concert database and about 15 million users, then moved into ticketing and merged with CrowdSurge in 2015. It sued Live Nation and Ticketmaster in 2016 over blocked US ticketing, closed ticketing in October 2017, sold the discovery business to Warner in July 2017 and remaining assets to Live Nation in January 2018 for a reported $110M. Incumbent power in ticketing capped the original plan, though the founders and investors had exits.

name: Splashup
long_description: Splashup, formerly known as fauxto, is an online image editing service that provides some advanced tools and is unique for its incorporation of image editing layer effects. The site is still in beta, and so does not offer full editing capabilities yet.
regions: Unspecified

name: Tsumobi
one_liner: Messaging.
long_description: Mobile applications have so far been nightmares to implement. It's often hard to gain adoption due to complicated installs and near impossible to get users to upgrade their version once the product has shipped. Tsumobi hopes to solve this problem by creating their own language. The new language will sit on top of J2ME and process applications downloaded (via URL) for Tsumobi enabled sites. This means that developers will be able to change Tsumobi applications on the fly and have Tsumobi enabled phones automatically get the updates just by visiting a link.
all_locations: Boston, MA, USA; Cambridge, MA, USA
regions: United States of America; America / Canada

name: Twitch
tags: Community; Gaming; Social Media; Video; Social Network
one_liner: A global community creating the future of live entertainment.
long_description: Twitch is the world’s leading video platform and community for gamers. More than 100 million gamers gather every month to broadcast, watch and chat about gaming. Twitch’s video platform is the backbone of live and on-demand distribution for leading video game broadcasters including casual gamers, pro players, tournaments, leagues, developers and gaming media organizations. Twitch is leading a revolution in the gaming community, working to create a participatory experience that transcends gameplay. Learn more at http://twitch.tv.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada; Remote; Partly Remote
target_customer: Gamers who stream and watch live gameplay, monetized through advertisers, subscriptions and bits; originally general lifecasting viewers
problem: Live streaming was hard to set up and had no community built for gamers; Justin.tv began as 24/7 lifecasting and later split out gaming.
business_model: advertising and viewer subscriptions with revenue share to streamers
product_category: live video streaming platform
founder_names: Justin Kan; Emmett Shear; Kyle Vogt
market_need_then: Lifecasting was a novelty in 2007; the gaming section later grew faster, with Twitch citing more than 20M gamers by 2012 per TechCrunch headline.
outcome_analysis: Justin.tv began as lifecasting in 2007, then spun out its gaming category as Twitch in June 2011 when gaming proved the real market. It raised a 15M USD Series B in September 2012 and a 20M USD Series C in September 2013, and Amazon announced its purchase for about 970M USD on 2014-08-25. Livestream (formerly Mogulus) was reviewed as a rival only in a May 2010 article, so it is noted here as a later competitor rather than a competitor at founding. Under Amazon it later cut roughly 400 roles in 2023 and over 500 in January 2024 to approach profitability.

name: View3
long_description: View 3, an active clad-alignment splicer with the world's highest fiber image magnification rate, is the most dependable fusion splicer.
regions: Unspecified

name: Virtualmin
long_description: Virtualmin is taking on the lack of innovation in the server admin programs, like Plesk, by making a more accessable version for pages managed by the non-technical crowd. The program will feature simple installs of popular programs like content management systems that often cost extra on other providers. It will also let you administer your website from your desktop and mobile device.
all_locations: San Francisco, CA, USA; Mountain View, CA, USA
regions: United States of America; America / Canada

name: Weebly
one_liner: Build a free website that grows with your business.
long_description:
Company Information
Weebly is a consumer service that gives people a surprisingly easy and affordable way to create a site that is as unique as they are. Weebly lets entrepreneurs start something and showcase their work. With a Weebly site, people can communicate with their clients, promote their works to potential buyers, share their story with like-minded people, and be an authority on personal and professional interests.

Weebly offers a range of pricing options, including a free plan and premium plans starting at $4/month. Weebly sites are optimized to work brilliantly across computers, phones and tablets.

Global Growth
Over 20million people around the world have started a site on Weebly
Weebly sites receive over 100,000,000 unique visitors each month
Weebly is offered in 11 languages: English, French, Spanish, Italian, German, Portuguese, Dutch, Chinese, JPese, Russian and Turkish

Weebly is privately funded by Sequoia Capital, Baseline Ventures, Ron Conway, and Y Combinator.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: Individuals and small businesses wanting a simple website or online store
problem: Building a website required HTML and design skills; non-technical people wanted a WYSIWYG drag-and-drop builder.
business_model: freemium SaaS subscriptions plus payments and add-ons
product_category: website builder
founder_names: David Rusenko; Chris Fanini; Dan Veltri
market_need_then: Penn State required students to keep online portfolios, giving an early use case; VentureBeat noted demand for WYSIWYG site building around 2007.
outcome_analysis: Weebly grew from a Penn State dorm project into a freemium site builder with over 20 million users, raised from Sequoia and Tencent, and was valued at about $455M in 2014 per press. Competition from Wix and Squarespace limited growth and Square bought it for about $365M in April 2018, below the earlier valuation.

name: Whitenoise
long_description: Whitenoise is like a social network for the music industry. It comes with specially made tools for bands, agents, publicists, and venues to manage each part of their business. Bands will be able to manage their cross country tours by map, using a venue search to find gigs in any town they're passing through. Venues will get access to a full list of artists in their area along with samples and ways to reach their agent to book a show.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada

name: WriteWith
long_description: Writewith is a collaborative writing web app, enabling you to easily flow through the steps of writing, editing, and publishing a document with a group. A document is started by uploading an existing document (.doc, .txt, .rdf) or just typing away. After the initial draft is completed, you can invite other editors by email and assign them tasks. Writewith has full version control and even lets you post comments to each other, making it possible to edit together in real time. Currently Writewith is in beta testing with 15 college newspapers including Stanford and two of Canada's largest college papers (which even includes a national newswire).
regions: United States of America; America / Canada

name: Zenter
one_liner: Zenter is the gmail of slides
long_description:
Zenter is an web based presentation app that promises to really take advantage of being online. Users will have the regular functionality of PowerPoint, but with the ability to directly add content from the web (Google Images). Each public slide show will also be put into a public library, for other users to remix or just drop into their show.

Zenter was acquired by Google in June, 2007.
all_locations: San Francisco, CA, USA; Mountain View, CA, USA
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: Individual and small-team users creating presentations online
problem: Presentation software was desktop-bound (PowerPoint) with no easy way to pull in web content or share and remix slide shows.
business_model: Free web app with a public slideshow library (no revenue model stated in sources)
product_category: Web-based presentation software
market_need_then: Google was building out Docs & Spreadsheets in 2007 and presentation sharing was reported as nearly the last missing piece of an online office suite; no user or revenue numbers were found.
outcome_analysis: Zenter was acquired by Google about six months into its life (announced June 2007, price undisclosed) as Google assembled its online office suite, and its technology and team fed what became Google Slides. Little is public about traction, so the outcome reads as a strategic early acquisition rather than a proven-demand story.

name: ZumoDrive
one_liner: Media in the cloud
all_locations: San Francisco, CA, USA; Burlingame, CA, USA
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: Consumers with large media libraries and multiple devices
problem: Music and files were stuck on one computer; users wanted to stream and sync media from cloud storage across devices.
business_model: Freemium cloud storage with paid tiers
product_category: Cloud storage and media streaming
market_need_then: Early 2009 coverage compared it with Dropbox and praised its price and features, showing demand for cloud media access.
outcome_analysis: Zecter built ZumoDrive for streaming and syncing media, launched in early 2009 into a field with Dropbox, SugarSync and Box.net, and raised a reported $1.5M Series A in December 2009. Motorola Mobility acquired the company on 2010-12-22, and the ZumoDrive service later ended. The exit looks like a technology and team deal rather than a win in the consumer storage race. Later entrants Dropbox, SugarSync and Box.net were the main rivals by 2009 and 2010.

name: iJigg/Top440
long_description:
iJigg is a social music site that lets users vote on submitted singles using Digg-like voting. The site's home page shows what popular or recent singles the iJigg community is "jigging." Users can rate songs, embed songs on MySpace or find similar music fans.

Competitors include Contrastream. Social music competitors include FineTune, Last.fm, Pandora and iLike.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada

name: 280 North
long_description:
280 North is a web application company based on their proprietary application framework, Cappuccino. Along with Objective-J, Cappuccino provides a complete toolkit to develop rich web applications. It's modeled after a proven desktop development environment, and has been released as an open source project under the LGPL.

280 North's first application, 280 Slides, enables anyone with a web browser to quickly and easily create beautiful presentations. 280 Slides takes advantage of the web by making it trivial to find and include great media in your presentation. We also built in advanced features like importing and exporting PowerPoint documents, so your data is always portable.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: Consumers and workers who make presentations in the browser, plus developers using the Cappuccino framework
problem: Presentation software required desktop installs; 280 Slides offered a Keynote like editor in the browser with PowerPoint import and export.
business_model: Free web application and open source framework; no revenue model found
product_category: Web based presentation app and web application framework
founder_names: Ross Boucher; Tom Robinson; Francisco Tolmasky
market_need_then: Online office apps were growing in 2008 with Google Docs and Zoho, and developers wanted desktop quality web apps; reviewers found 280 Slides elegant though less full featured than PowerPoint.
outcome_analysis: 280 North launched 280 Slides in June 2008 and built the Cappuccino framework, raising only about 250,000 in angel money. Motorola acquired it in summer 2010 for a reported 20 million to gain web app engineering talent; Motorola declined to disclose terms and later kept the Atlas tool private. It reads as a capital efficient technical team acquisition.

name: A Thinking Ape
one_liner: We build communities through massively multiplayer mobile games
long_description:
Proudly recognized as one of CANADA'S TOP SMALL & MEDIUM EMPLOYERS for 2018!

Mission: We build communities.

Surrounded by mountains and water in beautiful Vancouver, BC, we are smart people who like smart people. We create mobile games with a social core that engage players and provoke us with creative new problems. We value data, informal leadership and keeping it all balanced.

When we set out to make games with massive online communities, we knew that we first had to create the ideal environment for building ambitious things: a place where brilliant and inspiring people come together to build games that make millions of players happy. We realized that we needed to find incredibly talented people and get out of their way. Since then we've paid careful attention to how we like to work together - these are some of our guiding principles: Ownership; Have Wonderful Arguments; The Best Ideas Win; Keep Growing.

We are artists, designers, and engineers. We leverage our talent with small, independent teams. And we know that a happy builder is an efficient builder.
regions: Canada; America / Canada; Remote; Fully Remote
target_customer: Mobile gamers who play free to play social strategy games
problem: Founders started with a chat app (Chatterous), saw players using it alongside games, and moved to build social games with strong communities.
business_model: Free to play mobile games with in app purchases
product_category: Mobile social strategy games
market_need_then: Facebook and mobile social gaming were growing fast in 2009; the founders found players using their chat app as a game companion.
outcome_analysis: A Thinking Ape started in YC as a chat app, moved into social games in 2009 and says it was profitable and growing every year. Embracer Group acquired it through DECA Games in November 2020, one report putting the price near 105 million while another source says terms were undisclosed, so the price stays unrecorded here.

name: Anyvite
long_description: Anyvite is a free site dedicated to event invitation creation and group organization. Launched in 2008, Anyvite provides users with the most efficient way to create invitations as well as offers the tools necessary to organize and communicate with attendees throughout the event lifecycle.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada

regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: Bloggers, marketers and brands tracking conversations across blog comments and social media
problem: Blog comments were scattered across sites with no way to search or track them; BackType aggregated them and later offered social analytics.
business_model: Freemium search and analytics with an API; later aimed at brands
product_category: Social media and comment search and analytics
market_need_then: Blog commenting was a large conversation layer in 2008 and Twitter was rising; TechCrunch described BackType as Twitter for comments and found useful results for events such as TechCrunch50.
outcome_analysis: BackType launched in August 2008 as a search engine for blog comments, raised about 300,000 from True Ventures in March 2009, and widened to social analytics and big data tooling. Twitter acquired it in July 2011, discontinued the product and kept the team, and the Storm stream processor built there became an influential open source project; the price was not disclosed.

name: CO2Stats
one_liner: Social and environmental web analytics. Acquired in December 2016.
long_description:
CO2Stats aims to help website owners understand the electricity usage and related carbon emissions associated with site usage, and then helps site owners manage their carbon footprint.

The company calculates the greenhouse gas footprint of visits to your site, based on locations of your visitors and servers, computer types, window and monitor sizes, local fuel mixes, download sizes and times.

Every month CO2Stats purchase Green-E certified Renewable Energy Certificates to offset your site's CO2 footprint. Users can inspect your certificates and other environmental statistics by clicking on your CO2Stats badge.
all_locations: Boston, MA, USA; Cambridge, MA, USA
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: Website owners who wanted to measure and offset the carbon footprint of their traffic
problem: Sites had no easy way to quantify the emissions of serving visitors. CO2Stats estimated them and bought renewable energy certificates.
business_model: Flat rate service based on cumulative client power use, with a badge
product_category: Carbon footprint analytics and offsets for websites
market_need_then: Green web hosting and carbon offsets drew attention in 2008, but no demand metrics were found. BuiltWith shows 487 historical and 16 live sites using the widget.
outcome_analysis: CO2Stats launched its full service in August 2008 after YC S08, but no funding history or traction data was found. Directories say it was acquired in December 2016 without naming the buyer, so the deal terms and reason for the end of the product are not public.

name: Claimspotting
one_liner: Claim and conquer your city
regions: Remote; Fully Remote

name: Cloudant
one_liner: NoSQL Database-aaS.  Acquired by IBM in 2014.  Now IBM Cloud Data…
long_description:
Cloudant's distributed database-as-a-service (DBaaS) allows developers of fast-growing web and mobile apps to focus on building and improving their products, instead of worrying about scaling and managing their databases on their own.

We manage and distribute your data globally so you can grow more users, build more app features, and sleep more knowing we're keeping the servers up and humming.

Cloudant was founded in Cambridge, Massachusetts in 2008 by three MIT physicists who at the time were moving multi-petabyte data sets around from the Large Hadron Collider. Frustrated by the available tools for managing and analyzing Big Data in their research, the founders built a distributed, fault-tolerant, globally scalable data layer on top of Apache CouchDB.

The service has grown since then. The team now manages and serves mobile and web app data on behalf of thousands of developers and hundreds of customers to their users around the world. In 2014, the company was acquired by a global enterprise software & hardware vendor.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: Developers and companies building fast-growing web and mobile apps that need a managed, globally distributed NoSQL database
problem: Scaling and operating a distributed database is hard for small app teams. Cloudant ran and scaled CouchDB-style data stores as a service.
business_model: usage-based database-as-a-service (DBaaS) subscriptions
product_category: NoSQL database-as-a-service
founder_names: Michael Miller; Alan Hoffman; Adam Kocoloski
market_need_then: Founders came from large-scale physics data work (multi-petabyte LHC data per the YC page) and were frustrated with the tools available for managing big data. Web and mobile developers wanted databases that scale without in-house operations.
outcome_analysis: Cloudant started in the YC Summer 2008 batch with physicist founders who had handled huge data sets, built a distributed layer on CouchDB, and raised about $15.1 million in total by 2014 according to TechCrunch. The rise of mobile and web apps and the shift to managed cloud data created demand, and IBM bought the company in February 2014 for an undisclosed price to bolster its cloud portfolio after SoftLayer.

name: Deluux

name: JustSpotted
one_liner: Acquired by Google in 2011
long_description:
The artist-formerly-known-as Scoopler is a real-time search engine. It aggregates and organizes content being shared on the Internet as it happens, like eye-witness reports of breaking news, photos and videos from big events, and links to the hottest memes of the day. It does this by constantly indexing live updates from services including Twitter, Flickr, Digg, Delicious and more. When users search for a topic on Scoopler, they get the most relevant results, updated in real-time.

Scoopler has now become JustSpotted, a celebrity-tracking tool, meant to give fans an idea of what their favorite celebrities are up to at any given moment. JustSpotted, like Scoopler, is a data-aggregator, yet JustSpotted collects from Twitter, Facebook, and Foursquare -- alongside their own data theyâ€™ll be collecting from users who actual spot celebrities in the wild. All the information we aggregate is publicly available and you can even do a search on Twitter yourself and find sightings of celebrities. We're just the first people to organize it on a map and in such a way that it's easy to consume and ENJOY.â€

JustSpotted is about connecting with celebs. All the sightings on our website are naturally occurring events where an everyday person bumps into a celebrity as a chance occurrence. Back in the day, when you saw a celebrity while you were out and about the first thing you would have done was phone or text a friend. In the new age of social media, the first thing you do is share it on Facebook or Twitter. This phenomena is already happening.

The service, which launches the week of October 11, 2010, is the latest creation by AJ Asver, Dilan Jarawardane and Benjamin Tauber.

regions: United States of America; Denmark; America / Canada; Europe

product_category: Real-time social search, then celebrity sighting tracker

outcome_analysis: Scoopler entered a crowded real-time search field in 2009, raised a small seed from Ron Conway, Michael Birch and Avalon, then pivoted in 2010 to celebrity sightings. The pivot did not produce a lasting product. Google hired the three founders in July 2011 for Google+ and both services were closed, so the directory label of acquired is better read as a soft landing. The cause of the shutdown beyond the hire is not public.

On May 13, 2008, Omnisio launched a slide-syncing tool using SlideShare for slides and a host of video services.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada

Treehouse believes that understanding, communicating with and controlling technology is a fundamental skill that everyone should have the opportunity to learn. name: Airbnb
one_liner: Book accommodations around the world.
long_description:
Founded in August of 2008 and based in San Francisco, California, Airbnb is a trusted community marketplace for people to list, discover, and book unique accommodations around the world — online or from a mobile phone. Whether an apartment for a night, a castle for a week, or a villa for a month, Airbnb connects people to unique travel experiences, at any price point, in more than 33,000 cities and 192 countries. And with world-class customer service and a growing community of users, Airbnb is the easiest way for people to monetize their extra space and showcase it to an audience of millions.  

No global movement springs from individuals. It takes an entire team united behind something big. Together, we work hard, we laugh a lot, we brainstorm nonstop, we use hundreds of Post-Its a week, and we give the best high-fives in town. Headquartered in San Francisco, we have satellite offices in Dublin, London, Barcelona, Paris, Milan, Copenhagen, Berlin, Moscow, São Paolo, Sydney, and Singapore.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: Travelers seeking lodging and hosts monetizing spare space, two sided marketplace

Bookings fell almost 80 percent in the pandemic and it cut about a quarter of staff in May 2020, yet it listed on Nasdaq in December 2020 at a 47 billion dollar valuation and closed the first day near 100 billion.

name: Bump

long_description:
Bump was acquired by Google in 2013.  The Bump and Flock apps were shut down, but our unreleased Photoroll app went on to become the basis for Google Photos, which we led from inception to more than 1B users.

Bump let you exchange contact info and photos by bumping phones together.  Bump was one of the all-time top mobile apps, amassing more than 150M installs by 2013.  Flock was a semi-automated photo sharing app that figured out which photos you took with which friends and created private shared albums.

Bump was co-founded in 2009 and received funding from Y Combinator, Sequoia, and Andreessen-Horowitz. We were based in Mountain View, CA.
regions: United States of America; America / Canada
target_customer: Smartphone owners who wanted to swap contacts and later photos by physically bumping phones
problem: Exchanging contact details or photos between phones was slow and manual; Bump used the accelerometer and a server match so two phones bumped together swapped data.
business_model: Free consumer app; monetization was never achieved
product_category: Mobile contact and file sharing app, later photo sharing
market_need_then: Smartphone adoption was rising in 2009 and the iPhone App Store had just opened, but contact swapping was a convenience rather than a painful job. Demand showed as large install counts: the YC description states more than 150M installs by 2013.
outcome_analysis: Bump grew to more than 150 million installs on the viral gesture and raised about $19.5 million from Sequoia and Andreessen Horowitz, but never monetized. Apple's AirDrop in iOS 7 undercut the core use. Google acquired the company in September 2013 at a reported $30 million or more and shut Bump and Flock on 2014-01-31, while the unreleased Photoroll app became the basis of Google Photos, so the real value was the team and that product. Other success factor: the team's later product became Google Photos.

name: CarWoo

one_liner: We let you know where to go and what to get once you get there.…
long_description:
At its core GraffitiGeo allows users to leave brief reviews of restaurants, or for those too lazy to do that, to simply leave a "thumbs up" or "thumbs down" — it's like a highly condensed version of Yelp, or a "Digg for the world". These reviews and votes can be cast from the site's iPhone app or from the service's homepage. The homepage also features a stream of the latest comments to come in from other users, as well as a profile for each restaurant in the system that includes all of its votes and comments. There's also a nifty feature that lets you view a heatmap of your current region, so you can quickly figure out the hot spots in town.

The gameplay in GraffitiGeo gives you points for checking into certain locations, similar to FourSquare, but doesn't really let you do anything with them. With GraffitiGeo, you earn points for every action you take, be it voting on a restaurant or leaving a brief comment. Once you've reached a certain point threshold, you can use those points to start a "mob", which you can invite your friends to join. Mobs allow friends to pool their points, which can then be used to acquire territory, which corresponds to actual city blocks. Whenever someone votes on one of the restaurants on the block, the mob gets some street cred too. It's definitely going to be confusing at first, but it also brings a team element to gameplay.

market_need_then: Mobile local discovery was hot in 2009 with Foursquare and Gowalla growing and Yelp's iPhone app active; the founders argued long reviews did not fit the Twitter era.
outcome_analysis: GraffitiGeo launched in August 2009 as a thumbs up or down restaurant review app with a territory game, and Loopt, a fellow YC company, acquired it in October 2009 for undisclosed terms.
